train_texts: The case originated in six applications lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants complained that they had been dismissed by way of reprisal for belonging to a trade union and on account of its demands. The applications were allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) The Court declared admissible the applications (nos. 28955/06, 28957/06,. 28959/06 and 28964/06) and inadmissible the other applications. It also ruled on the admissibility and merits of the applications at the same time. The applicants sought to secure recognition by their employer of their special ‘salaried worker’ status. The applicants joined the union Nueva Alternativa Asamblearia (NAA) to defend their interests and those of the other delivery staff who were under pressure from the company P. to renounce their claim to salaried status. On [DATE_TIME] the applicants informed the company of the setting-up of a branch of the NAA. The composition of the Grand Chamber was determined according to the provisions of Article 26 §§ 4 and 5 of the Convention and Rule 24. The Court heard addresses by them. The trade union NAA published a [DATE_TIME] newsletter. On the cover of the newsletter, a cartoon with speech bubbles showed a caricature of the human resources manager, G., sitting behind a desk under which a person on all fours could be seen from behind. Inside the newsletter were two articles which vehemently denounced the fact that those two individuals had testified in favour of the company P. in proceedings that the applicants had brought against their employer. The newsletter was distributed among the workers and displayed on the noticeboard of the trade union. The applicants challenged that decision before Barcelona Employment Tribunal no. 17, which dismissed their claims and found that the dismissals were justified. The text was a response to what had happened during proceedings brought by the applicants before Barcelona Employment Tribunal no. 13. The article entitled “When you’ve rented out your arse you can’t shit when you please” read as follows: “If you belong to a works council and you have to sign agreements with your employers that will never be honoured, just to keep you quiet, and agree to changes that only benefit their cronies, and to pay cuts and other sell-outs, then you have the dubious merit of achieving the same level of infamy as politicians and policemen. You see, you shut up and you shrewdly agree to all sorts of shenanigans ...” You can see the injustices meted out on your colleagues, the totally irrational way of dealing with their problems and the constant persecution to which they are subjected, but say nothing, for fear of drawing attention to yourself. From time to time you have a pang of nostalgia and you would like to fart, but your sphincter is sealed, because you’ve rented out your arse and can’t shit when you please.” The employment tribunal observed at the outset that the cause of the dismissal was the content of the newsletter and not the applicants’ trade-union membership. It referred in its judgment to the exercise of the right to freedom of expression in the context of labour relations and to the fact that it was not unlimited. The High Court of Justice ruled that the cartoon was not in breach of freedom of expression. The court said that the publication of the cartoon did not violate the right to freedom of speech. The decision was made on the basis that it was in the public interest to publish the cartoon, and that it did not go beyond the bounds of the freedom of the press to do so. The Court said the cartoon violated the right of the public to be informed about the activities of the government, and the public’s right to know about the workings of government. The judge added that the decision was based on a principle of free speech, and not on the principle that the public should be able to know what the government is doing. Relying on Article 24 (right to a fair hearing) of the Spanish Constitution, the applicants lodged an amparo appeal with the Constitutional Court. The Constitutional Court found the appeal inadmissible for lack of constitutional content. The decision reads as follows: “... there is not enough evidence to show that the [appellants’] dismissal was an act of reprisal on the part of the respondent company’s’“ [DATE_TIME] decision of the High Court of Justice of Madrid was not pertinent,” it says. “In their allegations, the appellants have simply expressed their disagreement with the decisions rendered by the courts below, which found in decisions giving reasons and not being manifestly unreasonable” Constitution does not extend to absolutely vexatious expressions which are offensive or defamatory, says Court. Court: ‘Appellants’ right to freedom of expression has not been infringed. They used that right in an excessive manner by means of value judgments expressed through cartoons and comments that were offensive and humiliating for the persons concerned and impugned their honour and reputation.’ ‘Those cartoons were not necessary for others to form an opinion about the facts of which the appellants wished to complain, and were therefore gratuitous and not necessary in a trade-union context,' says Court of Appeal.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 47274/15) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicants alleged that they had been beaten and that pepper spray had been used on them by police officers who, owing to an inadequate investigation, had been neither identified nor punished. The German Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agents, Mr [PERSON] and [Person], of the Federal Ministry of Justice and Consumer Protection. The application was communicated to the Government on [DATE_TIME] and was heard in court on October 5, 2015. Police cordoned off the stands of the supporters of one of the teams, including both applicants, to prevent them from leaving the stadium. Some of these officers started hitting the spectators with their truncheons without any prior warning as soon as they reached them. The first applicant himself was hit with a truncheon on the head, which resulted in a bleeding laceration of 3cm behind his ear. Both applicants were able to identify their attackers as police officers, but were not able to distinguish them further, owing to their identical uniforms and the lack of identifying signs or name tags. The Government’s version of the subsequent events was that the blockade was lifted due to the aggressive behaviour of some of the spectators. The Government challenged the accounts of the applicants and submitted that there was no credible evidence that the applicants had deliberately been hit or harmed by police officers. The investigation was conducted by the unit of the [LOCATION] police responsible for offences perpetrated by public officials. The first applicant filed a criminal complaint against an unidentified police officer on [DATE_TIME]. He also submitted a medical certificate confirming a bleeding laceration on his head. Several other spectators at the match had also lodged criminal complaints against unidentified police Officers. The investigating division was also provided with a DVD showing excerpts of the video surveillance recorded by the riot control police at the football match. The officer in charge interviewed a total of twenty witnesses, including the applicants. The investigation had produced evidence that some of the police officers had used truncheons against spectators, including women and children, in a disproportionate way. The public prosecutor had been able neither to establish whether the applicants’ injuries had been inflicted by police officers nor to identify the suspects who had allegedly struck and used pepper spray on the applicants. It was established that the original video tapes and possible digital copies had already been deleted and that only the excerpts were still available. The investigating police unit was also provided with video surveillance recorded by the 23rd platoon of the 6th [LOCATION] public-order support force battalion. The applicants had requested that they be interviewed, as the evidence had suggested that the alleged perpetrators had belonged to one of these three squads. The Munich Court of Appeal declared the applicants’ application to force further enquiries inadmissible. The court interpreted the applicants' request as an application for criminal proceedings. The applicants appealed and pointed out that the members of the deployed squads had still not been questioned and that the inspected videos were fragmentary, but contradicted certain parts of the statements made by the squad leaders. The application was found to be an attempt to force criminal proceedings against an unidentified accused, which was not supposed to identify the accused or replace investigations. Only in a case where a public prosecutor’s office had entirely refrained from investigating a crime had a court the possibility to order an investigation. The applicants lodged a constitutional complaint, relying on Articles 2, 2, 19, and 103 of the German Basic Law (Grundgesetz) The court found that the investigations had been conducted diligently, but had not established sufficient suspicion of criminal conduct on the part of specific police officers. The court also found that it had not been necessary to question all the squad members who had possibly been involved. In its decision the Constitutional Court referred to the Court’s case-law concerning the procedural obligation of Article 2 of the Convention and, in particular, to the cases of McCann and Others v. [LOCATION] and [PERSON] v. [([DATE_TIME]), no. 33677/96, ECHR 1999‑VII). A subsequent appeal before the [LOCATION] general public prosecutor was to no avail. ‘’s office. ’s appeal against the decision was to be heard by a judge. The judge ruled the case was not a miscarriage of justice and ordered a retrial. The retrial was to take place at a later date. The case was dismissed and the case is now in the hands of an appeals panel. The decision was made after a hearing before a judge on December 8. The court was told that the case had been ‘inadmissible’. The appeal was dismissed on December 14. The verdict was returned in favour of the judge.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 25166/05) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The German Government did not make use of their right to intervene under Article 36. The Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the case at the same time. The applicant was born in [DATE_TIME] and lives in [LOCATION]. The applicant contended that he had not used any fog-lights. He claimed he had been driving at a maximum of 160 km/h. The Amstetten District Authority convicted the applicant of four traffic offences, namely speeding, breaching the requirement to drive in the right-hand lane, unjustified use of fog-lights and failure to carry his driving licence with him. The Independent Administrative Panel, sitting in camera, dismissed the appeal. Two police officers had been following the applicant over a stretch of more than 1,000 metres and had made consistent statements on the event. The applicant, on [DATE_TIME], lodged an appeal as regards the first three offences with the Lower Austria Independent Administrative panel. He did not appeal against his conviction for failing to carry a driving licence. He also did not request a hearing. This would have allowed it to examine his passenger and the police officers and to obtain an expert opinion. The Administrative Court partly quashed the Independent Administrative Panel’s decision. It upheld the conviction as regards speeding but quashes the sentence relating to this offence. It quashed conviction and sentence as to the unjustified use of broad-beam lamps. It refused to deal with the complaint relating to the conviction for breaching the requirement to drive in the right-hand lane pursuant to section 33a of the Administrative Court Act. In respect of the first two offences, the case was remitted to the Independent Administrative Panel, holding that the latter was obliged to hold a hearing, since none of the exceptions set out in the Administrative Offences Act had been present.

train_texts: Case originated in an application (no. 6563/03) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his conviction and fine for failing to reply to questions from financial investigators, where he had already been charged with the self-same offences, violated Article 6 of the convention. The parties did not file observations on the merits. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court. Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. The investigation was into whether any person had benefited from theft or false accounting. The maximum penalty for failure to attend an interview was [DATE_TIME] imprisonment or a fine not exceeding GBP 5,000. The applicant's solicitor sent a letter to the financial investigators indicating that the applicant's replies could become admissible evidence at a trial. He added that the purpose of the interview was to compel him to disclose his defence. The interview did not take place and the applicant was convicted of this offence in the Magistrates' Court and fined the sum of £1,500. The case was heard by the Independent Barristers' Association. Belfast County Court allowed the applicant's appeal against conviction, finding that the prosecution had not proved the absence of a reasonable excuse. Lord Justice Carswell considered, in the light of R. v. Hertfordshire County Council, ex parte Green Environmental Industries Ltd, that Article 6 § 1 of the Convention is directed towards the fairness of the trial itself. The judge took the view that once he had been questioned by the police and charged, the applicant had a right not to answer questions that would have tended to incriminate him. The only outstanding matter was whether the applicant should have attended the interview and then refused to answers questions, or, as he did, refuse to attend. The appeal was upheld, and the applicant's conviction confirmed. The criminal proceedings for false accounting and conspiracy to defraud were struck out on grounds of delay by the Belfast Magistrates' Court in [DATE_TIME]. The magistrate was asked by the office of the Director of Public Prosecutions to state a case for the Court of Appeal, but he died before having prepared the stated case. The application was decided in favour of the applicant, and he was convicted of false accounting. The conviction was confirmed and the application was dismissed. The appeal was dismissed and the case was dismissed, and an appeal was made against the conviction.
